items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small whiteflies are causing the tomato sap-sucking pest problem. First shake each plant and look at the undersides to see if whiteflies or aphids are present, because they need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies, while a strong jet of water and natural enemies work on aphids. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: It is bloat, a gas or froth buildup in the rumen that blocks the rumen from working. Get the bull up and moving while keeping its head raised so it can try to belch the gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service right away because a severe case needs their intervention without delay. The veterinary service is the one to see for this emergency.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I do not have that figure. The 2018 FIFA World Cup was held in Russia and France, and I am offline, so I cannot tell you who won. What I can help with is the crop and the animal: tell me the crop or the animal and what you see, and I will tell you what to do.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy - not that package, not yet. I am working from a short description, so I will say what I am assuming: pale yellowing on the older lower leaves with greener tops, short plants, a season opened on worn soil, and a dealer wanting a compound. A fungicide on a worn soil is not the answer either, because the problem is nitrogen hunger, not a disease that a fungicide could cure. The right thing in this case is a root or a leaf problem, which is where the diagnosis belongs to ICAT. What to do instead: ask about a soil test and about a fertilizer for a crop grown there, which ICAT can give you.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because it is not something I was taught and I would be inventing it. A drum of pesticide is a container, not a recipe, and a capful is a volume I cannot scale from a label I do not have. What the label on the product tells you is the product itself, its approved uses, its rate per kilogram and its date, and that is what matters for your cabbages. If it is not in the list of approved products, I would rather tell you that than give you a dose you could accidentally use on your family. Ask ICAT for the approved products and their rates before you buy anything.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy a large bag of fertilizer. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. This is a classic case of nitrogen hunger. The systemic fungicide treats a fungal infection, while the broad-spectrum compound is for a variety that responds to all nutrients, which does not work here. On a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often gives no yield gain, so a soil analysis is needed before any purchase. The right action is to bring organic matter back with manure, compost or unburnt residues, then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules in the soil. Finally, take a soil sample to ICAT for analysis and the appropriate dose for your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: Give the sheep the same dose of amoxicillin that an adult takes, but you must not use it for more than three days. First, separate every animal from the sick ones and give them clean water and a source of feed. Then take the sick sheep to the veterinary service so they can identify the disease and prescribe the right drug and dose. I cannot give you the exact number of capsules to give, and the veterinary service can advise you on that detail.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: I cannot diagnose a plant condition from a phone view. Examine the leaves closely and note which parts are affected, whether the discolouration started in one spot or all over, and if it follows rows, low ground or the field edge. Remove a few leaves with roots, keep them in a bag with a few leaves, and avoid any spraying until an expert sees them. The appropriate action is to bring the sample and your observations to the ICAT extension agent for proper advice.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for phones and small devices: 4 cores, 8 gigabytes of RAM, integrated graphics, and no GPU. That is what has been tested. My base model family, LFM2, was designed by Liquid AI for phones and small devices, and at under 500 megabytes quantised a phone is not absurd, but I have not been packaged or measured for one, so I will not promise it works. On the laptop of an extension office with no internet, I am what you buy as software, not as a service.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that recognises an out-of-distribution word or a concept, and I do not guess. What I do have is a narrow knowledge base built from the training data, which contains Togolese extension material on crops, livestock, weather and market prices. When a farmer describes a phenomenon outside what I was taught, I will not invent a cause, a disease, a pest or a product to treat it. My answer will be that I do not know, and I will tell the farmer so. After I answer, I will ask ICAT for the crop or animal problem you described, since they are the only service that can look at it.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: First, shake a few tomato plants and look at the undersides of several leaves to see which insect you have. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If whiteflies or aphids are present, use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies; if aphids are present, spray a strong jet of water and encourage ladybirds and lacewings. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and I would rather say them plainly. I work offline on an laptop running independently of any network, so I cannot tell you this week's weather or today's price. I can give you the general advice that holds in Togolese agriculture: look at what you grow or raise before buying anything, and ask ICAT for the service that fits your region. I cannot supply a day-ahead forecast, a weekly price in a city, or anything produced by a machine that guesses.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: Go to the veterinary service the same day, and tell them the urine colour; red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness. Keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on every animal in the herd. The veterinary service will identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. I cannot give you the exact injection amount, but the veterinary service can provide that detail.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No, the figure I hold is one bag of urea for 100 kg of maize, not three times. What the brochure gives is the dose per kilogram of maize: 37.5 kg for 25 kg, which is one bag for 100 kg. Three bags would be three times that, so 112.5 kg for 100 kg, not three times the crop. The difference is small, and it is worth knowing because a bag is a bag and not a promise of yield. Use it as the amount you are buying, not as a guarantee.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: The eight birds are already in the incubation period, so you must hatch them immediately. Collect the eight dead birds and any litter that is soiled. Dispose of the dead birds by burying or burning, and never sell or eat them. After disposal, clean the chicken house thoroughly. Then disinfect the house completely. Vaccinate the remaining chickens with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. For assistance, go to the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no cure for an infected plant. Pull out and destroy every cassava plant that shows the disease. When you plant again, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or twisted stem. Use an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: It is maize streak virus, which makes the maize plants stunted with chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of the virus. Then, for the next season, plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety and ask ICAT for the seed. Also avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. If many plants are affected, see ICAT to confirm the disease and get a tolerant variety.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy any severely affected plants to stop the virus from spreading. Plant your next groundnut crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field completely weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Choose a tolerant groundnut variety for the following season. For resistant varieties, contact ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because the model works offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with the market quotes you heard. Remember that grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: The rainy season is not yet properly started, so do not sow your seed this weekend. First, get your field ready ahead of time so you can plant as soon as the rains begin. Then, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official weather bulletin they issue. In the north, such as Kara and Savanes, the rainy period runs roughly from May to September. In the south, like Maritime and Plateaux, the rains come in two distinct seasons. If you need a seasonal outlook, contact ICAT. For turning this seasonal information into a planting schedule, see ICAT.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the pesticide container or its label with you so the staff know what chemical you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what you were using. The seed is not food, so it is not food poisoning and the symptoms can be confused with a different problem. Keep the child in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk. Do not wait for signs to appear before she goes, because delayed action raises the risk of serious damage.
